w01d1/brahmagupta.title: Brahmagupta's identity
transcript: In Example 1.1.3, the very first step is a monster. The book calls it Brahmagupta's identity, after the Indian mathematician who discovered it around the year 628.

Let's check it, one side at a time. Squaring two a n plus b m is like finding the area of a square with those two lengths along each side. There are four pieces: four a squared n squared, two copies of two a b m n, and b squared m squared.
On the right, two times a m plus b n, squared, gives two a squared m squared, plus four a b m n, plus two b squared n squared.
The product of the two brackets fills another box: b squared m squared, minus two a squared m squared, minus two b squared n squared, plus four a squared n squared.

Now add up the right side. Two a squared m squared cancels with its negative partner. So does two b squared n squared. What's left is exactly the left side. So the identity is true for every a, b, m and n.
So why use it? Because it makes both facts appear. a m plus b n is one, and b squared minus two a squared is zero. Substitute, and everything collapses to two.

Brahmagupta cared for a different reason. His identity turns one solution of x squared minus two y squared equals one into a bigger one. Three and two work. Feed them in, and out come seventeen and twelve. Again, and you get ninety nine and seventy.
And the fractions seventeen over twelve, then ninety nine over seventy, get closer and closer to the square root of two.
In Lean, you don't have to do any of this by hand. ring checks the whole expansion in one step.

w01d1/calc-chain.title: What is a proof by calculation?
transcript: Here's a puzzle. We have two numbers, a and b. We know that a minus b equals four, and a times b equals one. What is a plus b, all squared?
You could try to solve for a and b first. But there's a shortcut: rewrite what you want in terms of what you know.
Step one is pure algebra. a plus b, squared, always equals a minus b, squared, plus four times a b. No facts needed: expand both sides, and they match.
Step two is substitution. Our facts say a minus b is four, and a b is one. So we swap them in.
Step three is arithmetic. Four squared, plus four times one, is twenty.
Now read the whole chain, from the top left to the bottom right: a plus b, squared, equals twenty. And every link in the chain is either algebra, or substitution.
That's a proof by calculation. In Lean, you'll write exactly this chain, and justify each link the same way.

w01d1/reading-calc.title: Reading a Lean calc block
transcript: Here's the same proof, written in Lean. It looks different, but it's the same three steps.
The first two lines say what we're proving. h one and h two are names for the facts we were given: a minus b equals four, and a times b equals one. After them comes the goal.
The word calc starts a chain of equalities. Each underscore means: the expression we ended with, on the line before.
After each step comes its justification. By ring means: this step is pure algebra, so Lean checks it by expanding both sides.
By r w means rewrite, which is substitution. Rewriting with h one and h two swaps in the two facts, exactly like on paper.
If a justification is wrong, Lean underlines it in red. When every link checks out, the proof is complete.

w01d2/create-hypothesis.title: Making the facts appear
transcript: Here's the fact: x plus four equals two. And here's the goal: show that x equals negative two. The trouble is, the fact talks about x plus four, but the goal only has x.
So we make x plus four appear. Add four, and take away four. That's adding zero, so it's still just x.
Now x plus four sits right inside our expression. Swap it for two, because that's what the fact says it equals.
And two minus four is negative two. Done.
The same trick works with two facts at once. To get x from these two, add them up. The y's cancel, leaving x plus one.
So x is the first fact, plus the second, minus one. Swap in four and two, and x is five.
Every proof in this section asks the same question: how can I rearrange the goal, so that the facts appear inside it?

w01d2/long-division.title: Polynomial long division
transcript: In Example 1.3.10, the first line looks almost like magic. Where did z squared minus z plus one come from? The book's author found it with polynomial long division. Let's see how it works.

Start with plain numbers: thirteen seventy one, divided by twelve. Twelve goes into thirteen once, leaving one. Bring down the seven. Twelve goes into seventeen once, leaving five. Bring down the one. Twelve goes into fifty one four times, leaving three.
So thirteen seventy one equals twelve times one hundred fourteen, plus a remainder of three. Polynomials work exactly the same way.
Divide z to the fourth, minus z cubed, minus z squared, plus two z, plus one, by z squared minus two. Line up the terms by their power of z, like digits in columns.

How many times does z squared go into z to the fourth? z squared times. Multiply it back: z squared times the divisor is z to the fourth, minus two z squared. Subtract, and the leading term disappears.
Next, z squared goes into negative z cubed, negative z times. Multiply back: negative z cubed, plus two z. Subtract again.
Last, z squared goes into z squared once. Multiply back, subtract, and three is left over. Three has no z squared in it, so it's the remainder.
So the polynomial equals the divisor, times z squared minus z plus one, plus three. That's exactly the book's first line.
And our fact says z squared minus two is zero. That wipes out the whole first part, so the answer is just the remainder: three.
In the proof, you don't show any of this. It's scratch work for finding the identity, and ring checks it in one step. Try the same trick on exercise fourteen.

w01d3/inequality-chains.title: Which way does a substitution push?
transcript: Here are our facts: x plus three is at most two, and y plus two x is at least three. We want to show that y is bigger than three.
We build a chain, just like with equalities. But now each link can be equals, at least, or bigger than.
First, y equals y plus two x, minus two x. Then substitute: y plus two x is at least three, so the whole thing is at least three minus two x.

Next we want x plus three to appear. Three minus two x is the same as nine, minus two times x plus three. Now, careful. x plus three is at most two, but it's multiplied by negative two. Making it smaller makes the whole expression bigger. So this link is at least, not at most.
Nine minus four is five, which is bigger than three. Every link points the same way, so y is bigger than three.

Here's what goes wrong when the links disagree. n squared is at least twenty five, which is bigger than twenty one, which is at most two n plus eleven. Up, up, then down. That tells us nothing at all.
In Lean, rel makes each substitution and checks its direction for you. Push the wrong way, and it refuses.
